vulnerability.name: GHSA-fc5q-39xc-vjpf
vulnerability.description: picomatch: ReDoS through single-branch repeated extglobs (original range: all versions up to 4.0.7). GitHub WITHDREW this advisory on 2026-11-18 as 'not a security issue' (the upstream view: a glob pattern is trusted input).

statements.status_notes: Checked 2026-11-21 (plan W0). Advisory state: withdrawn by GitHub on 2026-11-18 (https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-fc5q-39xc-vjpf), and `npm audit` on the packed CLI reports 0 vulnerabilities; scanners that have not caught up may still list it. Our own code check, kept because the library behaviour has not changed: picomatch reaches the CLI only through fast-glob -> micromatch (packages/cli/src/utils/fs.ts calls fast-glob; ShipGuard never calls picomatch itself). The scan patterns are the constant '**/*' and the built-in default ignore list, which cannot carry an attacker glob. ONE route is open: src/core/ignore.ts selfArtifactIgnorePatterns() adds the policy values report.output and history.path, read from the scanned project's shipguard.policy.yml, to fast-glob's ignore list without escaping glob characters. A repository can ship a policy with an extglob such as +(*a) plus a long file name and make a scan spin (measured: a 29-character file name, about 20 s; each extra character multiplies it). Impact: a local CPU hang for whoever scans that repository; no data leaves the machine. So 'not reachable' is not yet true. This statement becomes not_affected (justification vulnerable_code_cannot_be_controlled_by_adversary) once those two values are escaped before they reach fast-glob; tests/release/openvex.test.ts keeps this status and the code in step. ignore.paths from the policy do not reach picomatch (they go through minimatch 11). Pinned: picomatch 2.3.2 (runtime, via micromatch; the newest 2.x) and 4.0.4 (dev tooling only) in pnpm overrides.
